ESTABLISHED FACTS & MEASUREMENTS:
  • On November 8, 1951, Eric Shipton and Michael Ward photographed ~12–13-inch footprints in the snow at the ~19,000-foot level of the Menlung Glacier; Sherpa Tenzing identified them as yeti tracks.
  • Sir Edmund Hillary's 1960 World Book Encyclopedia expedition examined the Khumjung monastery's 'yeti scalp' and identified it as serow skin.
  • Bryan Sykes's 2012–2013 Oxford-Lausanne Collateral Hominid Project analyzed 'yeti' hairs from Ladakh and Bhutan; re-analysis by Smithsonian researchers Gutiérrez & Pine attributed them to Himalayan brown bears.
  • Reinhold Messner proposed the chemo hypothesis: yeti sightings are the Tibetan brown bear, locally called 'chomo.'

NAMED WITNESS REPORTS:
  • Eric Shipton and Michael Ward (November 8, 1951) — Photographed ~12–13-inch footprints at the ~19,000-foot level of the Menlung Glacier (footprints, not a creature sighting)
  • N.A. Tombazi (1925) — Claimed a distant sighting of a large bipedal figure in Sikkim

PUBLIC INVESTIGATIONS:
  • World Book Encyclopedia expedition — Led by Sir Edmund Hillary, ?: The 'yeti scalp' was serow skin.
  • Oxford-Lausanne Collateral Hominid Project — University of Oxford / University of Lausanne (Bryan Sykes), ?: Alleged yeti hairs matched Himalayan brown bears, not an unknown primate.
